title: Workplace Compliance Training
description: Learn to recognize and respond to workplace compliance issues correctly

scenarios.customerSays: A coworker made a joke about someone's appearance in a team meeting.
scenarios.question: Is this harassment?

options.text: Yes, impact matters more than intent. If it made someone uncomfortable, it's harassment.
options.feedback: ✓ Correct! Our policy is clear: if a comment is offensive or creates discomfort, it's harassment regardless of whether it was meant as a joke.

options.text: It depends on who said it and who it was about.
options.feedback: ⚠️ Close, but not quite right. The INTENT of the joke-maker doesn't matter. What matters is the IMPACT on the person. If they felt uncomfortable, report it.

options.text: No, it was just a joke. People are too sensitive these days.
options.feedback: ❌ Incorrect. Our harassment policy covers all comments that create a hostile environment, including jokes. 'Just joking' is not an excuse. Report it to HR immediately.

scenarios.customerSays: You witness inappropriate behavior but the person involved apologized afterwards.
scenarios.question: Should you still report it?

options.text: Yes, report it to your manager or HR regardless of apology. They need to know for documentation purposes.
options.feedback: ✓ Exactly right! An apology doesn't erase the behavior. We need documentation to identify patterns and protect the organization. Report first.

options.text: If they apologized, you can let it go. No need to report.
options.feedback: ❌ Incorrect. Apologies don't prevent patterns. We MUST report to identify repeat offenders and protect our team. Your job is to report; HR's job is to investigate.

options.text: Talk to the person first before reporting.
options.feedback: ⚠️ You mean well, but confronting the person privately can escalate the situation. Instead, go directly to HR or your manager. They're trained to handle this.

scenarios.customerSays: HR is investigating a harassment complaint. What should you do if they interview you?
scenarios.question: What's the right approach?

options.text: Be honest, answer their questions directly, and don't discuss the investigation with coworkers.
options.feedback: Perfect! During an investigation: (1) Tell the truth, (2) Answer questions directly, (3) Keep it confidential - don't share details with others. This protects everyone.

options.text: Minimize what you saw to protect your coworker. They already feel bad.
options.feedback: ❌ Wrong. 'Protecting' someone by lying harms the organization. Tell the truth. HR's job is to be fair - truth is your best protection.

options.text: Tell your friends what happened so they know both sides of the story.
options.feedback: ❌ No. Investigations are confidential for a reason - to protect everyone involved. Gossiping interferes with the investigation and can constitute retaliation.

scenarios.customerSays: You notice a manager treating certain employees differently based on their age.
scenarios.question: What do you do?

options.text: Document what you observe and report it to HR. Discriminatory treatment is against policy, regardless of how 'nice' the manager is.
options.feedback: ✓ Exactly right! Discrimination based on age, race, gender, etc. is illegal AND against our policy. Report it. You're being a good teammate by protecting everyone.

options.text: Mind your business. It's not your problem.
options.feedback: ❌ It IS your responsibility. We all have a duty to prevent discrimination. Staying silent enables it. Report to HR.

options.text: Talk to the manager privately about it.
options.feedback: ⚠️ Good intent, but managers may not recognize their own bias. Going to HR first is better - they're trained to investigate fairly and address patterns.

masteryLevels.description: You're learning our compliance policies. Review the feedback carefully, especially for questions you answered incorrectly.
